Recalling the obligation under Article 3 paragraph 1 subparagraph b of the Convention to address risks and impacts arising from activities within the lifecycle of artificial intelligence systems by private actors to the extent not covered in subparagraph a of that provision in a manner conforming with the object and purpose of the Convention, the Union declares that it will apply the principles and obligations set forth in Chapters II to VI of the Convention to activities of private actors placing on the market, making available and using artificial intelligence systems in the European Union through the implementation of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act). Other relevant Union acquis may also apply to these activities and contribute to the implementation of the principles and the obligations of the Convention. (Declaration contained in the instrument of approval handed over on 15 May 2026; original English.)

European Union, Article 32(1): Declaration of the European Union on the Territorial Scope of Application pursuant to Article 32 paragraph 1 of the Convention. Pursuant to Article 32 paragraph 1 of the Convention, the Union declares that, with regard to the competence of the Union, the Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law is to apply to the territories in which the EU Treaties are applied pursuant to Article 52 of the Treaty on European Union and under the conditions laid down in, inter alia, Article 355 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. Norway, Article 3(1)(b): In accordance with Article 3, paragraph 1.b, of the Convention, the Kingdom of Norway declares that it shall apply the principles and obligations set forth in Chapters II to VI of this Convention to activities of private actors. Ukraine, Article 3(1)(b): In accordance with Article 3, paragraph 1.b, of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law, Ukraine declares that it shall take other appropriate measures with respect to the activities of private entities not covered by Article 3, paragraph 1, subparagraph “a”, of the Convention in order to fulfill the obligation set forth in Article 3, paragraph 1, subparagraph “b”, of the Convention in a manner consistent with the object and purpose of the Convention. ai_provisions: Operative paragraph 1 — recognises AI's potential to contribute to human rights and sustainable development, while acknowledging risks to the enjoyment of human rights.

Operative paragraph 2 — affirms that the design, development, deployment and use of AI must be consistent with international law, including international human rights law and international humanitarian law as applicable.

Operative paragraphs 3–7 — AI governance under human-rights law; legislative and regulatory measures; participation of developing countries; access to information; human dignity, equality, privacy, transparency, explainability, accountability, accessibility, human oversight and effective remedies.

Operative paragraph 8 — States should refrain from or cease uses of AI that cannot be operated consistently with international human rights law or that pose undue risks, including systems whose capabilities could reasonably be expected to cause loss of human control.

Operative paragraphs 9–10 — human-rights due diligence and impact assessments; meaningful human oversight, information, human review and effective remedies where AI plays a material role in decisions affecting rights.

Operative paragraphs 11–13 — freedom of opinion and expression, privacy, differentiated impacts on vulnerable groups, and the responsibility of business enterprises under the Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights.
Operative paragraphs 14–17 — AI literacy, international cooperation and capacity building, digital public goods and open models, and coherence among international initiatives.
Operative paragraphs 20–23 — a panel discussion at the 65th session on AI capacity building and the AI divide; an OHCHR report to the 66th session; the Council remains seized of the matter.

relevance.excluded_scope: Military AI is excluded: Article 3(2) limits the Organization's functions exclusively to the civilian domain. The Agreement establishes an organization and a cooperation framework; it does not itself set product rules, prohibitions, testing standards or a judicial dispute-settlement mechanism. Disputes are to be settled by consultation (Article 13).
relevance.reason: The constituent treaty of the first intergovernmental international organization specifically dedicated to artificial intelligence. It establishes WAICO as an independent intergovernmental organization with international legal personality, headquartered in Shanghai, with a Council and a Secretariat, and limits its functions exclusively to the civilian domain of AI (Article 3(2)). It is subject to ratification, acceptance or approval and enters into force on the deposit of the third such instrument (Article 15). It is a treaty, not a political declaration, and it is the second AI-specific treaty in the corpus alongside CETS 225.

instruments.status_note: Treaty, binding on States that become parties, but not in force as of 23 November 2026. Article 15 requires three instruments of ratification, acceptance or approval for entry into force. China's National People's Congress approved ratification on 6 November 2026; no deposited instrument was verified, so the record does not count a ratification and the map records signature only. China's MFA reports 38 founding members, but the primary signing records individually identify 37: 29 States at the 16 July 2026 ceremony and eight later signatories named on 30–31 July 2026. The October 2026 progress report says nine States joined after the initial 29; eight are named, so one of the nine remains unnamed. Bangladesh is not that member: on 1 August 2026 its Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced that Bangladesh would join "initially as an observer", after the signature period had closed. Article 11 requires an observer application and approval by the Council, and no admission is recorded; observers are not Founding Members under Article 10. Singapore has been reported as considering an invitation to join; it is a Pax Silica signatory and not a WAICO member. The discrepancy is recorded, not resolved. The Government of China is the depositary under Article 18; no public depositary register or notification of a deposited ratification was located.
